DEVIATION REPORT
Cross-Border Data Transfer Agreement — Counterparty Markup Analysis
Data Privacy & Cybersecurity Practice

I. INTRODUCTION AND SCOPE

This deviation report reconciles the counterparty's markup of the Cross-Border Data Transfer Agreement against our client's original draft and the firm's negotiated-position playbook for cross-border data transfer matters. The analysis incorporates the transfer impact summary and partner instructions applicable to this engagement, and evaluates each counterparty-introduced deviation for consistency with applicable data protection regulation (including GDPR, the EU-U.S. Data Privacy Framework, and applicable national data transfer laws), firm precedent, and market practice.

The operative agreement contains representations and warranties, affirmative and negative covenants, conditions to closing, indemnification, and termination provisions. Counsel flagged specific provisions requiring close analysis against firm precedent and market practice, including deviations introduced by the counterparty's latest markup.

Nine deviation items were identified across three principal areas: (1) the indemnification mechanics, (2) the definition of Material Adverse Effect (MAE), and (3) the survival/limitation period for core representations. Each deviation is analyzed below against the original draft position, the playbook standard, and the applicable regulatory framework.

II. SUMMARY OF DEVIATIONS

The counterparty's markup introduces three material deviations from the original draft and playbook that require reconciliation:

Deviation Category       | Counterparty Proposal                                    | Risk Level
-------------------------|-----------------------------------------------------------|------------
1. Indemnification       | Cap reduced; basket converted from deductible to         | HIGH
   Structure             | tipping basket                                            |
2. MAE Definition        | Carve-outs added for regulatory action of the kind        | HIGH
                         | at issue in this matter                                    |
3. Survival Clause       | New limitation period shortens survival for the core      | MEDIUM
                         | representations                                            |

Each deviation is addressed in detail below.

III. DEVIATION 1 — INDEMNIFICATION STRUCTURE

A. Original Draft / Playbook Position

The original draft and the firm's data-privacy-cybersecurity playbook for cross-border data transfer agreements adopt a standard indemnification structure whereby (i) the seller's aggregate indemnification liability is capped at an agreed percentage of the transaction consideration, and (ii) claims are subject to a deductible basket, meaning the indemnitee must absorb losses up to a stated threshold before making any recovery.

The deductible-basket structure is the market-standard and firm-preferred position in data transfer transactions. It provides certainty, aligns risk allocation with the economics of the deal, and is consistent with the treatment of similar cross-border data transfer transactions in the firm's precedent bank.

B. Counterparty Markup

The counterparty's revision introduces two changes to the indemnification mechanics:

(i) The indemnification cap is silently reduced below the original agreed level, thereby limiting the counterparty's aggregate exposure for breaches of data transfer, privacy, and cybersecurity representations and warranties.

(ii) The deductible basket is converted to a tipping basket, meaning that once the threshold is met, the indemnifying party is liable for the full amount of losses (including the amounts up to the threshold) rather than only losses in excess of the deductible.

C. Analysis and Impact

Impact on Data Transfer Risk. A cross-border data transfer agreement inherently involves elevated regulatory risk. The transferring party's obligations under GDPR Articles 44–49, the EU-U.S. Data Privacy Framework, and applicable local transfer restriction regimes carry a real prospect of regulatory action and third-party claims. Silently reducing the cap while simultaneously converting the basket from a deductible to a tipping structure shifts additional allocation of cost away from the transferring party and onto the receiving party. This is inconsistent with the allocation of risk contemplated in our original draft, which placed responsibility for transfer compliance with the party best positioned to control the transfer mechanics—the transferring party.

Basket Mechanics. The conversion from a deductible to a tipping basket is particularly consequential where regulatory exposure from a data transfer event can be concentrated. Because a tipping basket triggers full recovery once the threshold is met, the counterparty effectively creates a large aggregate exposure point at the threshold, and then dilutes the incremental exposure by limiting total recovery through the reduced cap. The combination of a reduced cap and a tipping basket allows the counterparty to contain its maximum exposure at a lower level while creating the appearance of enhanced indemnitee protection through the tipping mechanism.

D. Recommendation

• Reject the reduction of the indemnification cap. The cap should be restored to the level set forth in the original draft and firm playbook. A reduction of the cap is not market-standard for cross-border data transfer agreements where the representations relate to compliance with data protection law, cybersecurity standards, and cross-border transfer mechanisms.

• Reject the conversion to a tipping basket. Counter or propose restoration of the deductible-basket structure, consistent with firm precedent for data transfer matters. If the counterparty insists on a tipping basket, seek an increase in the threshold amount to compensate for the increased recovery exposure, and ensure the basket is expressed to apply per-claim as well as in the aggregate.

• If the counterparty will not accept the deductible-basket structure, as a fallback negotiate a cap that is increased to reflect the incremental exposure created by the tipping-basket mechanics.

IV. DEVIATION 2 — MATERIAL ADVERSE EFFECT (MAE) DEFINITION

A. Original Draft / Playbook Position

The original draft's MAE definition is consistent with firm precedent: it excludes ordinary and expected regulatory actions, but does not carve out regulatory actions that are specific to the data transfer matter at issue. The playbook position is that the MAE definition should not be drafted so broadly as to exclude a material adverse change arising from the very regulatory risks that are the subject of the transaction—i.e., the risk that a data protection authority takes enforcement action against the transferring party's cross-border data transfer program.

B. Counterparty Markup

The counterparty adds carve-outs to the MAE definition for "regulatory action of exactly the kind at issue in this matter"—meaning regulatory actions relating to cross-border data transfers, data protection authority enforcement proceedings, or changes in applicable transfer-restriction law that arise between signing and closing.

C. Analysis and Impact

The proposed carve-out has a direct and material adverse impact on the value and purpose of the MAE clause. In a cross-border data transfer transaction, the single most material risk is that a data protection authority—such as a European supervisory authority enforcing GDPR, or a national regulator enforcing a local data-localization or transfer-restriction regime—takes adverse action against the transferring party's transfer mechanism. The contemplated carve-out would exclude precisely such regulatory action from the MAE definition, meaning the buyer/receiving party could not terminate for a material adverse change in circumstances that fundamentally undermines the transferred data processing.

The carve-out is drafted to be precisely targeted at the core risk the parties allocated in the original draft and playbook. This is not a legitimate exclusion of ordinary-course or expected regulatory activity. Rather, it eviscerates the MAE protection for the exact risk scenario the transaction was designed to address: the viability and continuity of the data transfer program.

D. Recommendation

• Reject the proposed MAE carve-out in its entirety. The carve-out for "regulatory action of the kind at issue in this matter" is outcome-determinative and would defeat the fundamental purpose of the MAE clause.

• If the counterparty presses for some accommodation, propose a narrow and balanced alternative that: (i) excludes regulatory action that was known, disclosed, or reasonably foreseeable as of the signing date; but (ii) preserves the right to terminate for a material adverse change arising from new or escalated regulatory enforcement action, changes in law, or reversal of adequacy or derogation determinations applicable to the specific transfer mechanism.

• Confirm that the carve-out applies only to ordinary-course regulatory engagement and does not extend to enforcement action, revocation, suspension, or invalidation of transfer mechanisms (e.g., invalidation of Standard Contractual Clauses by a court or regulator, or suspension of a Data Privacy Framework certification).

V. DEVIATION 3 — SURVIVAL / LIMITATION PERIOD

A. Original Draft / Playbook Position

The original draft provides for a survival period for core representations—including the data privacy, cybersecurity, and cross-border transfer compliance representations—consistent with the firm's playbook for data transfer transactions. The playbook standard is a survival period of at least [X] years for fundamental and regulatory representations and warranties, reflecting the extended regulatory exposure inherent in data transfer matters where non-compliance may not be discovered immediately and where enforcement actions can arise years after the closing.

B. Counterparty Markup

The counterparty introduces a new limitation period that shortens the survival of the core representations relative to the original draft. The shortened period provides that the data transfer and privacy representations survive for a reduced duration, with the effect that the receiving party loses its right to bring a claim for breach of the core data protection representations after the shortened period expires.

C. Analysis and Impact

The shortened survival period is particularly problematic in the data privacy and cybersecurity context for several reasons:

First, breach of data protection obligations frequently has a long tail. Regulatory investigations by data protection authorities can extend for multiple years, and supervisory authority enforcement proceedings often come to light only after a significant delay. A shortened survival period significantly undermines the utility of the core representations by depriving the indemnitee of recourse for breaches discovered after the limitation window has closed.

Second, the core data privacy and cybersecurity representations are fundamental to the value of a cross-border data transfer transaction. If the transferring party's compliance program is defective, or if the transfer mechanism becomes non-compliant, the economic and regulatory consequences may not be fully known for a prolonged period. Shorter survival for these representations is inconsistent with market practice for regulatory representations in data-driven transactions.

Third, the shortened period may conflict with applicable regulatory retention and diligence requirements, potentially exposing the receiving party to continued liability for operations conducted with non-compliant transfer mechanisms without adequate contractual recourse.

D. Recommendation

• Reject the shortened limitation period for core representations. Insist on the survival period set forth in the original draft and playbook for the data privacy, cybersecurity, and cross-border transfer representations.

• If the counterparty will not accept the full original survival period, negotiate a tiered approach: a shorter survival for general representations and warranties, but a longer (or indefinite, where permitted by applicable law) survival for the fundamental representations—including data privacy and cross-border transfer compliance representations—consistent with firm precedent and market practice.

• Consider adding a "discovery" extension, whereby the survival period is tolled or extended with respect to any claim reasonably discoverable by the receiving party after the survival date, subject to the longer of the stated period or an agreed period following discovery.

VI. ADDITIONAL OBSERVATIONS AND RECONCILIATION NOTES

A. Playbook Conformance

Beyond the three primary deviations, the markup was reviewed against the firm's data privacy cybersecurity playbook for cross-border data transfer agreements. No other material deviations were identified in the counterparty's revision. The counterparty's acceptance of firm-standard provisions in the remaining sections (including representations concerning data processing records, security incident notice, sub-processor notice, and the general framework for cross-border transfer documentation) is noted.

B. Transfer Impact Summary

Consistent with the transfer impact summary for this engagement, the three deviations identified above would, if accepted, materially shift the allocation of cross-border data transfer risk away from the transferring party. The combination of a reduced cap with a tipping basket, an MAE carve-out for the exact regulatory action of concern, and a shortened survival period would collectively diminish the value of the transaction protections at precisely the points where data transfer regulatory risk is greatest. These changes are conceptually internally consistent on the counterparty's side—together they systematically reduce the counterparty's exposure to the regulatory risks of this transaction.

C. Partner Instructions

In accordance with partner instructions, all three deviations are to be treated as items requiring affirmative negotiation. None should be deemed acceptable without an explicit commercial agreement to the contrary. The partner-level guidance emphasizes that the MAE carve-out is the single most consequential deviation and is not acceptable in any form, while the indemnification cap reduction and basket conversion, and the survival period change, each merit resistance at the term-sheet level and, if necessary, escalation to the transaction committee.

VII. RECOMMENDED NEGOTIATION POSITION SUMMARY

Deviation            | Position                    | Fallback                                        | Escalate?
---------------------|-----------------------------|-------------------------------------------------|----------
1. Indemn cap        | Reject; restore             | Increase cap in exchange for tipping basket     | Yes
   reduction         | original cap                | mechanics                                        |
--------------------------------------------------------------------------
1(b). Basket         | Reject; restore             | Accept tipping if threshold raised and          | Yes
   conversion        | deductible basket           | cap restored                                      |
--------------------------------------------------------------------------
2. MAE carve-out     | Reject in entirety;         | Narrow carve-out for known/disclosed            | Yes — 
                     | no acceptable form          | regulatory matters only                          | per partner
--------------------------------------------------------------------------
3. Survival          | Reject shortened            | Tiered survival with longer (or indefinite)     | Yes
   period            | period                      | survival for core regulatory reps                 |

VIII. CONCLUSION

The counterparty's markup introduces three material deviations that, taken together, would systematically shift cross-border data transfer risk to the receiving party. The indemnification cap reduction and deductible-to-tipping basket conversion, the MAE carve-out for regulatory action, and the shortened survival period for core representations collectively undermine the protective structure of the agreement as originally drafted and as required by the firm's playbook.

Each deviation is rejected or targeted for strong counter-negotiation as set forth above. The receiving party should be prepared to hold firm on the MAE definition in particular, which is the single most consequential deviation in the markup. If the counterparty continues to insist on the proposed terms at closing, the matter should be escalated for commercial review.

Prepared by Data Privacy & Cybersecurity Practice
Harrow & Vane LLP
